questions.q: Why does a single straggler node slow down an entire synchronous data-parallel training job?
options: Straggler nodes automatically disconnect from the job
An all-reduce is a synchronization point every rank must reach before any can proceed, so the job's effective throughput is bounded by its single slowest rank in every step
Synchronous training ignores slow ranks and proceeds without them
It doesn't -- only crashed nodes affect job throughput
questions.explain: Because every rank must arrive at the all-reduce before any can proceed, the slowest rank determines how long every other rank waits -- making overall throughput bounded by the slowest member, not the average.

questions.q: Which of the following is a cause of straggler behavior that does NOT involve a node crashing or hanging?
options: A process segmentation fault
A kernel panic that halts the operating system
A corrupted checkpoint file
Thermal throttling from marginally worse cooling, causing a node to clock down under sustained load
questions.explain: Thermal throttling is a straggler cause where the node remains functional and never crashes -- it simply runs slower due to clock reduction under thermal limits, unlike crashes or kernel panics.

questions.q: Why is per-rank, per-step timing a better straggler-detection signal than aggregate job throughput?
options: Aggregate throughput and per-rank timing always show identical information
Aggregate throughput is always more precise than per-rank timing
Aggregate throughput shows that something is wrong but not which specific node is responsible, while per-rank timing identifies the slow node by comparing ranks against each other
Per-rank timing cannot be measured in a distributed training job
questions.explain: Aggregate throughput reveals that the job has slowed but not the cause; per-rank timing isolates which specific rank is consistently slower than its peers, pinpointing the straggler.

questions.q: What is a limitation of using a noisy-neighbor explanation for straggler behavior on a shared cluster?
options: A noisy neighbor always causes a permanent hardware failure
Noisy neighbors never affect training jobs
Noisy neighbors only affect jobs running on a single GPU
The affected node can be intermittently slowed by another job's resource competition without being unhealthy itself, making the straggler behavior transient rather than a persistent hardware problem
questions.explain: A noisy-neighbor straggler is caused by resource contention with another workload, so the affected node is not itself unhealthy -- the slowdown can be intermittent and tied to what else is running on shared infrastructure.

questions.q: Why do most large LLM training runs stay synchronous and manage stragglers operationally rather than switching to fully asynchronous training?
options: Fully asynchronous training introduces gradient staleness that complicates convergence, so synchronous training with operational straggler management (draining, timeout tuning) is generally preferred
Asynchronous training guarantees faster convergence in every case
Asynchronous training is not possible on GPU clusters
Synchronous training has no synchronization overhead at all
questions.explain: While asynchronous training avoids the synchronization bottleneck in principle, it introduces gradient staleness that complicates convergence, so most large runs stay synchronous and handle stragglers through draining and timeout tuning instead.
